terms.definition: The two-step process that turns a gene's DNA instructions into an actual protein: transcription copies the gene into mRNA, then translation reads that mRNA to build the protein.
terms.function: Converts the genetic information stored in DNA into the working proteins that carry out nearly every task inside a cell.
terms.whereItIs: Transcription happens inside the nucleus; translation happens afterward at a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the process, often called the central dogma of molecular biology, that connects your DNA to every physical trait and function your body has.

terms.definition: The step where an enzyme unwinds a short piece of DNA and builds a matching, disposable mRNA copy of it.
terms.function: RNA polymerase unwinds a short stretch of the DNA double helix, reads one strand as a template, and links RNA bases together to build a matching mRNA strand.
terms.whereItIs: Inside the nucleus, at the 'transcription bubble' near the base of the DNA helix, where the two DNA strands visibly separate and the new mRNA thread begins.
terms.whyItMatters: This step keeps the master DNA copy safe in the nucleus while still letting the cell act on its instructions — without it, the cell would have to risk its one permanent genetic library every time it needed a protein.

terms.definition: The finished mRNA copy exits the nucleus through a pore in its envelope and travels into the cytoplasm.
terms.function: Carries the transcribed instructions out of the nucleus, through a nuclear pore, to where a ribosome is waiting in the cytoplasm.
terms.whereItIs: At the nuclear pore gap in the nuclear envelope, where the mRNA tube passes from inside the translucent nucleus to outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: This handoff physically connects the two halves of the central dogma — without mRNA making this trip, the instructions copied from DNA would never reach a ribosome.

terms.definition: The ribosome clamps onto the mRNA strand and reads it three letters (one codon) at a time.
terms.function: Moves along the mRNA strand, reading each 3-base codon in order and matching it, via tRNA, to the correct amino acid to add next.
terms.whereItIs: At the two-lobed ribosome assembly in the cytoplasm, clamped on the mRNA where the thread passes through the cleft between the large and small subunits.
terms.whyItMatters: This is where the genetic code actually gets decoded into a physical sequence of amino acids — the direct link between a gene's sequence and a protein's structure.

terms.definition: As the ribosome reads each codon, it links the matching amino acid onto a growing chain, which becomes the finished protein.
terms.function: Links each newly matched amino acid onto the end of a growing chain in the exact order the mRNA codons specify, until a stop codon ends the chain.
terms.whereItIs: Along the bead chain arcing up and away from the top of the ribosome, near where the last few beads begin to coil.
terms.whyItMatters: This finished chain is the protein — the actual working molecule (enzyme, structural fiber, hormone, antibody) that carries out the instructions originally copied from DNA.

terms.definition: The molecule that stores a cell's genetic instructions, kept safely inside the nucleus.
terms.function: Serves as the permanent template that transcription reads to produce mRNA; never leaves the nucleus and is never directly used to build a protein.
terms.whereItIs: Coiled inside the nucleus, including the short unwound stretch shown at the transcription bubble.
terms.whyItMatters: DNA is the master copy of every instruction the cell has — protecting it while still letting the cell act on it is the entire reason transcription exists.

terms.definition: The compartment inside a cell where DNA is stored and transcription takes place.
terms.function: Encloses and protects the DNA, and is where RNA polymerase builds mRNA before that mRNA exits through a nuclear pore.
terms.whereItIs: The large translucent membrane-bound compartment on the left side of the scene, with a single visible pore where the mRNA exits.
terms.whyItMatters: Compartmentalizing DNA inside the nucleus is what makes it possible to keep the master genetic copy separate from, and protected from, the rest of the cell's activity.

terms.definition: The disposable RNA copy of a gene that carries instructions from the nucleus to a ribosome.
terms.function: Acts as the working copy of a gene's sequence, carrying the instructions RNA polymerase transcribed out of the nucleus to a ribosome for translation.
terms.whereItIs: The single continuous tube running from the transcription bubble inside the nucleus, out through the nuclear pore, to the ribosome in the cytoplasm.
terms.whyItMatters: mRNA is single-stranded, uses uracil instead of thymine, and is temporary — it lets the cell build proteins without ever risking the permanent DNA copy.

terms.definition: The enzyme that builds an mRNA strand by reading a DNA template during transcription.
terms.function: Unwinds a short stretch of DNA and links RNA bases together, one at a time, to build a strand of mRNA that matches the DNA template it's reading.
terms.whereItIs: Sits at the unwind point of the transcription bubble, at the base of the DNA helix inside the nucleus.
terms.whyItMatters: Without this enzyme, the instructions stored in DNA could never be copied into a usable working form.

terms.definition: The molecular machine, found in the cytoplasm, that reads mRNA and assembles amino acids into a protein during translation.
terms.function: Clamps onto mRNA, reads it one codon at a time, and links the matching amino acids into a growing protein chain.
terms.whereItIs: In the cytoplasm, outside the nucleus, clamped onto the mRNA strand.
terms.whyItMatters: The ribosome is the physical site where the genetic code gets translated into a real, working molecule — a protein.

terms.definition: A sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for one specific amino acid (or a start/stop signal).
terms.function: Acts as the ribosome's basic unit of instruction; each codon tells the ribosome exactly one amino acid to add next, or when to start or stop.
terms.whereItIs: Read in order along the mRNA strand as it passes through the ribosome.
terms.whyItMatters: Codons are the actual 'letters' of the genetic code — the specific 3-letter grouping is what makes translation possible at all.

terms.definition: A small RNA molecule that carries one specific amino acid and matches it to the correct codon on the mRNA.
terms.function: Delivers the correct amino acid to the ribosome for each codon being read, matching its own anticodon to the mRNA codon.
terms.whereItIs: Ferries amino acids to the ribosome as it moves along the mRNA strand.
terms.whyItMatters: tRNA is the translator between the genetic code (codons) and the physical building blocks (amino acids) — without it, the ribosome would have no way to match the two.

terms.definition: A small building-block molecule; chains of amino acids, linked in a specific order, fold up to form a protein.
terms.function: Links onto the growing protein chain in the order specified by the mRNA's codons, one amino acid per codon.
terms.whereItIs: Delivered by tRNA to the ribosome, then linked into the bead chain arcing away from the ribosome.
terms.whyItMatters: The specific sequence of amino acids determines how a protein folds and what job it can do, so getting this order right is the entire point of translation.

terms.definition: The codon AUG, which marks the point where the ribosome begins building a protein.
terms.function: Signals the ribosome where to start reading and also codes for the first amino acid (methionine) in the new chain.
terms.whereItIs: The first codon read once the ribosome clamps onto the mRNA and begins translation.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a defined starting point, the ribosome wouldn't know where a gene's instructions actually begin along the mRNA strand.

terms.definition: One of three special codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) that signal the ribosome to stop adding amino acids.
terms.function: Tells the ribosome the protein chain is complete and triggers its release from the ribosome.
terms.whereItIs: The final codon read at the end of a gene's mRNA sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: Without a stop signal, the ribosome would keep adding amino acids past the point where the actual protein's instructions end.
